title: Youth justice centre order (YJC) / youth residential centre order (YRC)
statement: If a custodial sentence is appropriate for a young offender on conviction (or appeal) in a higher court, the court may make a YJC or YRC order instead of imprisonment; these are not sentences of imprisonment. (The Manual also gives a Magistrates’ Court maximum for these orders: see yjc.maximum.) Purposes: punish while promoting rehabilitation and separating the young offender from experienced adult offenders.

refs.q: Regardless of the charge, if a custodial sentence is deemed appropriate for a young offender on conviction (or appeal) in a higher court, that court may make a youth justice centre order (‘YJC’) or a youth residential centre order (‘YRC’). These youth detention orders are not sentences of imprisonment.

rules.statement: For a Category A serious youth offence, or a Category B serious youth offence where the offender has previously been convicted of a Category A or B serious youth offence, the court must be satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist before making a detention order. The requirement does not prevent a non-custodial sentence if detention is not justified and the purposes can be met without confinement. The Manual says it might be seen as a presumption in favour of imprisonment (though that does not appear to have been the legislative intent) and is probably better viewed as Parliament’s intent that such offenders be imprisoned in appropriate cases rather than detained. Whether circumstances combine to be exceptional is fact dependent. The Manual does not list which offences are Category A or B serious youth offences (flag.serious_youth_offence_categories).

rules.statement: Maximum detention under either order, regardless of the number of convictions in the proceeding: four years in the County or Supreme Court; two years in the Magistrates' Court. The maximum also caps cumulation across occasions: if the offender is already serving youth detention, cumulation orders operate only up to the maximum. (Actual detention exceeding the maximum by declining to credit pre-sentence detention is technically possible, but that authority has since been confined.) Whether an earlier sentence counts in full or only its unexpired part is not stated; (app policy) the cap across occasions is applied to what cumulation achieves: the unexpired part of the detention being served plus the part of the new detention cumulated on it (new detention wholly concurrent with it — the presumption, yjc.concurrency — adds nothing), with a caution where counting the whole earlier term would exceed the maximum (flag.youth_detention_cap_across_occasions).
rules.logic: the effective period of the youth detention (YJC/YRC) imposed in this proceeding, after concurrency and cumulation (concurrent terms are not added; imprisonment imposed concurrently or cumulatively is not counted): error if it exceeds 48 months (Supreme/County Court) or 24 months (Magistrates’ Court); where youth detention is already being served (intake.status_at_offence), add to its unexpired part only the part of the new detention cumulated on it (app policy): error if that total exceeds the maximum; if counting the whole earlier term instead of its unexpired part would exceed it → caution (flag.youth_detention_cap_across_occasions); new detention wholly concurrent with the detention being served adds nothing

rules.statement: Youth detention terms are presumed concurrent with any other uncompleted detention or imprisonment unless the court orders otherwise; detention served concurrently with imprisonment is served in a prison until the imprisonment has been served. The presumption does not apply to escaping from or damaging a youth justice or youth residential centre: those sentences must be served cumulatively on other detention unless the court orders otherwise and gives reasons for concurrency. Similarly, there is a presumption of cumulation on any uncompleted sentence in default of payment of a fine or sum of money. If a higher court imposes imprisonment exceeding the maximum possible YJC term, it can be impracticable also to impose a YJC on another charge. (Commencement where imprisonment is also being served: the Manual’s wording reads inverted, flag.youth_detention_commencement_wording.)
rules.logic: escape from / damage to a youth justice or youth residential centre with its detention made concurrent with other detention → error unless reasons for concurrency are stated (run in audit.cumulation_exceptional_circumstances); imprisonment on one charge above the YJC maximum with a YJC proposed on another charge → caution (impracticable: Cairns)

rules.statement: Aggregate detention may be imposed in largely the same manner as aggregate imprisonment: for two or more offences founded on the same facts, or forming or part of a series of offences of the same or similar character, even if the underlying offences are representative or rolled-up charges. It cannot exceed the total of the separate sentences of detention that might have been imposed, and the court must announce the decision in open court, give reasons and explain its effect. Pre-detention custody for the offence (or proceedings arising from it) must be declared as time served unless the court orders otherwise; this does not apply to periods under one day, a sentence under one day, or a period already declared under another sentence or a Court Secure Treatment Order. With continuous custody since arrest on a series of offences, the whole period from arrest counts even if the offender is not convicted of the offence underlying the first arrest. (Compare psd.declare and psd.exclusions for imprisonment.)

rules.statement: Although not without ambiguity (flag.cyfa_disposition_power), it appears that a higher court sentencing a child may impose a CYFA disposition or, if those are inadequate, any sentence under the Act. General deterrence is not relevant to sentencing children under the CYFA, but applies (possibly ameliorated by youth) if adult custody is necessary. In CNK v The Queen, a child in the Supreme Court because charged with attempted murder, acquitted of that charge and convicted of other uplifted offences, had to be sentenced on the remaining uplifted charges as if exclusively governed by the CYFA; how that holding sits with the power to impose a sentence under the Act where CYFA dispositions are inadequate is not stated (flag.general_deterrence_childrens_court_charges). Rehabilitation is the cardinal principle of the youth justice system. The standards the reasoning must apply are in youth.higher_courts_principles and youth.cyfa_hierarchy.

rules.statement: Where a higher court considers a CYFA disposition, the dispositions are hierarchical: a disposition lower in the list may not be imposed unless the court is first satisfied that none of those preceding it is appropriate. In ascending order: dismissal without conviction; dismissal with an undertaking; dismissal with an accountable undertaking; good behaviour bond; fine; probation; youth supervision order; youth attendance order; youth control order; YRC order; YJC order (the first four without conviction; fine, probation and youth supervision order with or without conviction; the last four — youth attendance, youth control, YRC and YJC orders — only on conviction).
rules.logic: if a CYFA disposition is proposed: the reasoning must say why each preceding disposition is not appropriate (error if it skips up the hierarchy without reasons); a youth attendance, youth control, YRC or YJC order made without a conviction → error (the Manual lists these four only as “convicting the child and making …”)

refs.q: Meaning a court may not impose a sentence in a given paragraph of the following list unless it is first satisfied that it is not appropriate to impose one given in any preceding paragraph.

The dispositions available under the CYFA, in ascending hierarchical order, are: • dismissing the charge, without conviction; • dismissing the charge and ordering the giving of an undertaking, without conviction; • dismissing the charge and ordering the giving of an accountable undertaking, without conviction; • placing the child on a good behaviour bond, without conviction; • imposing a fine, with or without conviction; • placing the child on probation, with or without conviction; • releasing the child on a youth supervision order, with or without conviction; • convicting the child and making a youth attendance order; • convicting the child and making a youth control order; • convicting the child and making a YRC order; • convicting child and making YJC order.

rules.statement: Sentencing a child or young offender in a higher court: (1) the CYFA considerations — the family relationship, living at home, continuing education, training or employment, minimising stigma and the suitability of the sentence; if appropriate, the child’s awareness that they must bear responsibility for illegal acts; protection of the community from the child’s violent or other wrongful acts (in all cases for a Category A or B serious youth offence, otherwise if appropriate); and, if appropriate, deterring the child from offending in remand, youth residential or youth justice centres — must be considered “as far as practicable”, meaning to the maximum extent possible; they are policy objectives, and the sentence must fit the young offender as much as (or maybe more than) it fits the crime. (2) The normal considerations apply but may be subordinate while the court first assesses whether a CYFA disposition is adequate. (3) Whether youth detention or adult custody is adequate may depend on whether the maximum youth detention is sufficient punishment for the seriousness, criminal history, rehabilitative assistance in the youth system, the public nature of the offending and the circumstances of and harm to the victim. (4) General deterrence is not relevant when sentencing a child under the CYFA, but if adult custody is necessary it applies, although it may be ameliorated by youth. (5) Where rehabilitation is paramount, the purposes might be met without confinement and a CCO takes on greater importance. (6) Rehabilitation is the cardinal principle; only for the gravest offending with almost no prospect of rehabilitation may youth not mitigate; its weight may need modification for serious and dangerous offending such as terrorist activity, where general deterrence and denunciation become primary.

refs.q: In determining an appropriate sentence, a reviewing court must, ‘as far as practicable,’ consider: • the need to strengthen and preserve the relationship between the child and their family; • the desirability of allowing the child to live at home; • the desirability of allowing the education, training or employment of the child to continue; • the need to minimise stigma to the child; • the suitability of the sentence to the child; • if appropriate, the need to ensure that the child is aware they must bear responsibility for any illegal action by them; • the need to protect the community, or any person, from violent or other wrongful acts of the child — • in all cases where the sentence is for a Category A serious youth offence or a Category B serious youth offence; or • in any other case — if it is appropriate to do so; and • if appropriate, the need to deter the child from offending in remand centres, youth residential centres or youth justice centres.

rules.statement: It is an error to view a CCO as serving an entirely rehabilitative purpose, and its rehabilitative purpose cannot cure a manifestly inadequate sentence. statement: A fine may be imposed with or without conviction, in addition to or instead of another sentence; not for Level 1 offences; for Level 2 offences only in addition to imprisonment (unless otherwise stated or a body corporate); not if a dismissal, discharge or adjournment would achieve the purposes. Main purposes: punishment and deterrence. A fine includes costs but not restitution or compensation, costs of such applications, costs between parties in a civil proceeding, third-party costs, or payments to a charitable or community organisation. The Manual’s own penalty tables print “Level 1 – life and fine not exceeding 5000 penalty units” for some DPCSA offences, which the 12.1 bar does not reconcile (flag.level1_fine_dpcsa); and it does not say whether the Level 1/2 rules apply to life or 25-year maxima printed without a level (flag.fine_unlabelled_life_25_maximum).

It cannot be imposed as an alternative, unless otherwise stated or if the offender is a body corporate. Lastly, a fine may not be imposed if the purposes for which a sentence is imposed can be achieved by dismissal, discharge, or adjournment.

rules.statement: Relevant to amount: maximum fine; gravity; financial circumstances and ability to pay; natural person or body corporate; loss, destruction or damage to property caused; value of benefit derived; time already in custody for the offending or because of immigration status. title: Dismissal without conviction
statement: Solely a non-conviction order. The discretion arises only when the charge is proved and the plea was a proper one. The Manual then says the offence 'must' be able to be characterised as 'trifling', the circumstances clearly indicating it would be manifestly unfair and unreasonable to penalise and stigmatise the offender (e.g. trivial offending, or a conviction that might disqualify the offender from their profession), but also that dismissals "may also be granted" where strong steps towards rehabilitation, or previous good character and post-offence conduct, would make a conviction disproportionate. Whether these are alternative grounds or the trifling requirement always applies is not resolved (flag.dismissal_trifling_requirement). No conditions may be attached, but compensation or restitution may be ordered separately. A dismissed charge cannot be revived. A dismissal is not a conviction for any purpose except as the Act provides: it has the same effect as a recorded conviction for appeals against sentence, variation or breach proceedings, proceedings for a subsequent offence, and subsequent proceedings for the same offence (so a prior dismissal can count in later sentencing: intake.criminal_history).

title: Release on adjournment (adjourned undertaking), with or without conviction
statement: The court may adjourn and release the offender on an undertaking with conditions, with or without conviction, for up to five years. It is only available if the offender first agrees to give the undertaking (agreement given because imprisonment is a realistic alternative is still valid). Mandatory conditions: attend court if called on (and at any adjourned hearing), be of good behaviour, observe any special conditions; a justice plan condition may be attached (lasting for the adjournment or two years, whichever is shorter; the CCO condition is worded differently: flag.justice_plan_request). The court must be satisfied of guilt and have regard to the nature of the offence, the offender’s character and past history, and the impact of a conviction on economic or social wellbeing or employment, balanced with general deterrence; it should expressly say whether a conviction is recorded. An adjourned undertaking is a “sentence”. Usually made for minor offences, but not if that would breach the fundamental principles or purposes; it may be imposed for serious offences in exceptional circumstances (e.g. marginally excessive self-defence in a family violence context, serious psychiatric illness, the wellbeing of children or a partner as carer, unusual child pornography possession, assistance to authorities), and other mitigation may also lead to one (e.g. significant delay, intellectual disability or mental health issues, youth or advanced age, an unwilling accomplice, immigration detention). On compliance the offender is discharged (if convicted) or the charge dismissed (if not).

title: Residential Treatment Order (RTO)
statement: Detention for up to five years in a residential treatment facility, designed for people with an intellectual disability who have committed serious sexual or other violent offences. Eligible offences: sexual assault, sexual assault by compelling sexual touching, or a “serious offence”, which includes (the Manual does not say the list is complete: flag.rto_serious_offence_list) (murder, manslaughter, child homicide; causing serious injury offences; threats to kill; rape, rape by compelling sexual penetration, assault with intent to commit a sexual offence; familial sexual penetration offences; sexual abuse or penetration of a child under 16; kidnapping and abduction for sexual purposes; armed robbery; repealed equivalents; conspiracy, incitement or attempt). Only if the DHS Secretary specifies that the offender is suitable for admission and the planned services are available. Not if a less restrictive sanction is more suitable; an intention to impose one may constitute special reasons for not imposing a mandatory term. Eligible offences cannot be a gateway for ineligible ones, which need separate sanctions that do not interfere with the RTO; separate RTOs cannot be cumulated (additional orders are redundant). Length: a sentence, so no more severe than necessary; it may exceed the minimum period recommended in a pre-sentence report and need not track the imprisonment otherwise appropriate, so long as it is proportionate. Pre-sentence detention cannot be declared for the RTO offence if already declared for other offences dealt with at the time. If the order is cancelled and the offender re-sentenced, a new s 6AAA declaration must be made if relevant.

title: Court secure treatment order (and court assessment order)
statement: Orders for mentally ill offenders, only if no less restrictive means are reasonably available. A court secure treatment order (CSTO) requires: (1) that but for the mental illness the court would have imposed imprisonment; (2) consideration of the person’s current mental condition, physical and mental health, forensic history and social circumstances; (3) a psychiatrist’s examination and report (with any other evidence) satisfying the court that the person has a mental illness (actual, not merely apparent as for a court assessment order), needs treatment to prevent serious deterioration or serious harm, will receive it, and has no less restrictive means reasonably available; (4) a report from the authorised psychiatrist of the service recommending the order and stating facilities are available. The illness need not have caused the offending. All relevant sentencing considerations apply. Duration must not exceed the imprisonment that would otherwise have been ordered (so that notional term must be considered); a life-duration order is possible for offences punishable by life. A non-parole period must be fixed “as if it were a term of imprisonment” (the Manual does not say how this works with the ch 8 rules — no non-parole period under 12 months (8.3.1), a discretion between one and two years and, for two years or more, an exception where an npp is inappropriate (8.3: npp.must_fix_two_years): flag.csto_npp_short_terms). On discharge, the unexpired period takes effect as imprisonment served in prison unless paroled, so the offender may serve some or virtually all of it in prison.

rules.statement: “Mental illness” is a medical condition characterised by a significant disturbance of thought, mood, perception or memory. A person is not mentally ill only because of listed matters, including political, religious or philosophical opinions, sexual preference, gender identity or orientation, promiscuity, immoral, illegal or antisocial conduct, intellectual disability, drug or alcohol use, economic or social status, cultural or racial group, family conflict, or previous treatment for mental illness. Drug or alcohol consumption is not sufficient, but its serious temporary or permanent physiological, biochemical or psychological effects may indicate a mental illness. The offender need only be assessed as mentally ill at the time of sentencing (the illness need not have caused the offending).

title: Drug and Alcohol Treatment Order (DATO) — Drug Court only
statement: Made only by the Drug Court Division of the Magistrates' or County Court. Eligibility: plea of guilty to at least one imprisonable offence within the Drug Court’s jurisdiction; conviction; dependency on drugs or alcohol that contributed to the offence (balance of probabilities); otherwise an unsuspended prison term would be appropriate (no more than 2 years in the Magistrates’ Court, 4 years in the County Court); assessment report ordered and received; appropriateness; written agreement to the order and to comply with the treatment and supervision part. Excluded: schedule 1 sexual offences (24.5 says a Drug Court order is not available for “a sexual offence”, citing the same provision, s 18Z(1)(a)(i), and the Manual does not list schedule 1: a DATO is excluded (error) where the user states the offence is a schedule 1 sexual offence; otherwise the exclusion is unresolved, a caution — for the 24.1.1, 24.1.2 and 24.1.4 offences the app does not propose a DATO unless the user states the offence is not a schedule 1 sexual offence (app policy, following 24.5’s words), and for the child abuse material and sexual servitude offences the user is asked: flag.dato_sexual_offence_scope), offences involving the infliction of actual bodily harm (but the Magistrates’ Drug Court may make a DATO where satisfied the harm was of a minor nature: fn 2834), offences under ss 10–10AE; an offender on parole or subject to a higher court sentence. Prior imprisonment, prior dependency-driven offending or prior non-compliance with bail or sentence does not bar a DATO. One DATO may cover multiple offences, but an offender can be subject to only one DATO at a time. The custodial part is a term of imprisonment equal to the sentence that would otherwise be imposed (no non-parole period; automatically suspended; maximum 2 years Magistrates’ Court, 4 years County Court); it must not be lengthened merely to allow treatment, nor artificially decreased to fit under the maximum. It will generally be prudent to declare eligible pre-sentence custody when the DATO is imposed. Purposes include recovery through judicially supervised therapeutic rehabilitation, community protection from substance-driven offending and reducing health risks; rehabilitation and community protection have greater importance than the other purposes.

statement: A court considering a YJC or YRC order must first order a pre-sentence report. A YJC order cannot be made for an offender under 15 at sentence, and a YRC order cannot be made for one who is 15 or over. Youth detention may be served concurrently or cumulatively on imprisonment, but if a higher court imposes imprisonment exceeding the maximum possible YJC term it can be impracticable also to impose a YJC on any other charge. Time after a young offender is allowed to go free (for any reason) until their return to custody, and after an escape or failure to return until apprehension or surrender, does not count and the sentence is suspended. An aggregate detention order need not identify the separate events, the sentences that would have been imposed on each charge, or whether they would have been concurrent or cumulative. Custody referable to the proceedings must be declared as time served unless the court orders otherwise.

title: Boulton in detail: suitability, parsimony, punishment, deterrence, rehabilitation, protection; the discretion; combinations
statement: Boulton appears to accept that suitability derives from the Act (the offender’s circumstances and capacity to comply, subject to proportionality); an offender is not unsuited merely because a disadvantage or disability makes compliance difficult. The Manual says it also appears the Court might be of the view that some incarceration is required for intentionally causing serious injury, reckless conduct causing injury (such as driving while intoxicated), or a series of linked domestic-violence incidents over some hours. The first question is whether any feature requires the conclusion that imprisonment is the only option — i.e. whether confinement is necessary and, if so, the minimum term. Although a CCO’s punitive effect never equals imprisonment, it is a “significant punishment”, not a “mere slap on the wrist”: its conditions are coercive and restrictive, an intensive compliance period increases the burden, and every CCO is punitive every day it is in force; after a term of imprisonment the punitive purpose should be progressive and supervision should reduce over time. In Dyason the argument that Boulton required reconsideration of the primacy of deterrence for white-collar offending was rejected. Most youthful offenders disengage from crime quickly, so a CCO should avoid alienating them; the circumstances always control. Community protection is not legislatively primary for a CCO but remains the ultimate purpose. Boulton does not fetter the discretion, is no “Get Out of Jail Free” card, and does not require a CCO that would not reflect the objective seriousness and the offender’s circumstances; current sentencing practice informs the first question. Reasonable minds differ on the longest term before a combination is more severe than necessary; a short term of imprisonment may be needed for purposes a CCO cannot serve. A CCO and a non-parole period should ordinarily be alternatives. The discretion to “otherwise order” on time served is not unfettered; the custodial period is fixed after deducting time served (even if concurrent with another offence).

title: DATOs in detail: transfer; the custodial part and activation limits; sanctions; graduation; cancellation; reports; subsequent charges
statement: Before transfer the Magistrates’ Court must be satisfied the accused may be eligible, without assessing sentence. The court must impose a term of imprisonment as the custodial part, which is not served unless activated; activation is not a fresh sentence (no occasion for a s 18 declaration). The maximum activatable custody excludes declared pre-sentence detention and sanction time, (with a worked example) and in some cases is reduced by the excess days of operation of the treatment part; a shorter activation involves listed factors, and compliance is assessed by effort. Conditions run for the treatment and supervision part unless cancelled; core conditions include attending the Drug Court. A sanction may activate the custodial part for 1–7 days (if satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of non-compliance; after notice; in a specified kind of facility), served only if the period or total of unserved activated periods is at least seven days. Graduation cannot be granted once the program conditions have ceased. Cancellation under s 18ZP requires a listed ground on the balance of probabilities (cancellation for reoffending under s 18ZN requires satisfaction beyond reasonable doubt: order.dato.activation_and_cancellation); compliance is not measured by duration; unwillingness and non-compliance are not to be conflated; the remaining custodial part is calculated first and compliance taken into account; notice is required, and the parties must have an adequate opportunity to call evidence and make submissions on both the decision to cancel and its consequence (not necessarily in separate stages, though a two-step process is preferable). Assessment reports are filed and served, and disputed parts are tested before use. If no DATO is imposed the court must take one of the listed courses. On a new offence, an immediate term may be subsumed within the remaining custodial part, failing which the treatment part is cancelled; a Magistrates’ Court has no jurisdiction over a summary or triable-summarily charge against a County Court participant and must transfer it to the County Court Drug Court for sentencing (for a not-guilty plea see flag.dato_county_court_subsequent_charge).

statement: Sentencing children operates within a largely separate system (Children’s Court Bench Book); the Manual covers children and “young offenders” sentenced in the higher courts and youth detention as an alternative. title: CCO pre-sentence report: purpose; an assessment order does not presume a CCO
statement: Except for a CCO limited to 300 hours or less of community work (11.4.2.1 says “less than 300 hours”: flag.cco_work_only_300_hours), a pre-sentence report must establish suitability, available facilities and appropriate conditions; it should cover treatment and programs and how long support and monitoring are likely to be needed. Presuming a CCO will follow a positive assessment “fundamentally misconceives” the Act and Boulton; the discretion is not fettered.

refs.q: Except as just noted with respect to a CCO limited to 300 hours or less of community work, a court must order a pre-sentence report to establish the offender’s suitability for a CCO, ascertain that necessary facilities exist, and gain advice regarding the most appropriate conditions to be attached to the CCO.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.1 – Prerequisites and limits > 11.1.1 – Pre-sentence reports

refs.q: Information regarding the availability of treatment and programs is critical and should be included in the pre-sentence report.

title: CCO mandatory conditions
statement: Every CCO requires the offender not to commit an imprisonable offence during the order; comply with the regulations; report to and receive visits from the Secretary; report to the specified community corrections centre within two clear working days; notify changes of address or employment within two clear working days; not leave Victoria without permission; and comply with the Secretary’s directions.

refs.q: CCOs have mandatory conditions that attach to each order. These require that an offender must: • not commit an offence punishable by imprisonment during the period of the order; • comply with any obligation or requirement prescribed by the regulations; • report to and receive visits from the Secretary during the period of the order; • report to the community corrections centre specified in the order within two clear working days after the CCO comes into force; • notify the Secretary of any change of address or employment within two clear working days after the change; • not leave Victoria without the permission of the Secretary; and • comply with any direction given by the Secretary to ensure the offender complies with the order.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.1 – Mandatory conditions

title: CCO treatment and rehabilitation condition
statement: The court must specify one or more types (drug/alcohol assessment and treatment including testing, residential withdrawal or rehabilitation, medical, mental health, offending-behaviour programs, other programs including employment, educational, cultural and personal development). It must address the underlying causes of offending and the pre-sentence report’s recommendations. Completion of programs may reduce unpaid work hours. Compliance is generally assumed, though a CCO may be inappropriate if there is no realistic prospect of compliance.

refs.q: A court may require an offender to undergo specified treatment and rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.2 – Treatment and rehabilitation conditions

refs.q: The court must specify one or more of the following types of treatment and rehabilitation: • assessment and treatment (including testing) for drug and/or alcohol abuse or dependency; • assessment and treatment (including testing) at a residential facility for withdrawal from or rehabilitation for alcohol and/or drug abuse or dependency; • any medical assessment and treatment, including general or specialist treatment or treatment in a hospital or residential facility; • mental health assessment and treatment, including treatment in a hospital or residential facility; • programs that address factors relating to the offender’s offending behaviour. • any other treatment and rehabilitation the court considers necessary and is specified in the order, including employment, educational, cultural and personal development programs consistent with the purpose of the condition.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.2 – Treatment and rehabilitation conditions

refs.q: When imposing a treatment and rehabilitation condition, the court must have regard to the need to address the underlying causes of the offending, and to the recommendations, information and matters identified in the pre-sentence report in relation to the treatment and rehabilitation of the offender.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.2 – Treatment and rehabilitation conditions

refs.q: The court may structure a CCO so that successful completion of rehabilitation programs entitles an offender to a commensurate reduction in any unpaid community work hours they are required to complete.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.2 – Treatment and rehabilitation conditions

refs.q: In assessing whether to impose a CCO, the sentencing judge should generally assume that the order will be complied with, and that any initial difficulties will abate once treatment gets underway. refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.2 – Treatment and rehabilitation conditions

title: CCO supervision and non-association conditions

title: CCO residence restriction/exclusion, place/area exclusion and curfew: consistency with intervention orders
statement: A residence restriction or exclusion condition must not be imposed if inconsistent with a family violence intervention order, personal safety intervention order or child protection order; a place or area exclusion condition, and a curfew condition, must not be imposed if inconsistent with a family violence or personal safety intervention order. Safety of co-residents and employment effects may be considered. With a residence condition the offender may not move unless the court first varies the CCO. Whether a condition is inconsistent with an order is a judgement on the orders’ terms, so the auditor applies it (caution where the intake records an existing FVIO, PSIO or child protection order affecting the offender and the conditions may conflict).

title: CCO alcohol exclusion condition: content, purpose, and when it may moderate sentence
statement: Excludes the offender from nightclubs, bars, restaurants, cafés, reception or function centres, major events and bar areas, and from drinking in other licensed premises (exemptions and hours may be specified). Primary purpose is community protection; it may aid rehabilitation and can be punitive. An offender contending it has additional punitive impact must say so expressly, with evidence, and address the s 89DE(5) exemption; the court should then make a finding on its punitive extent and explain its effect on sentence. Note: the Manual prints these principles under the CCO condition heading but introduces them as applying “to an alcohol exclusion order” (the ancillary order, whose exemption is s 89DE(5)); how far they govern the CCO condition is not stated (flag.aeo_principles_placement; see anc.alcohol_exclusion_order).

refs.q: The court may attach an alcohol exclusion condition to address the role of alcohol in the offender’s offending behaviour.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.8 – Alcohol exclusion condition

refs.q: its primary purpose is to protect the community, which it does by limiting the opportunity for the offender to consume alcohol in venues where others are present and who may be harmed if the offender becomes intoxicated
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.8 – Alcohol exclusion condition

refs.q: if the offender wishes to contend the order has an additional punitive impact, they must do so expressly, provide evidence supporting the contention, and address whether s 89DE(5) is amelioratory
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.8 – Alcohol exclusion condition

refs.q: if an offender expressly contends their sentence should be moderated because of the order, the sentencing court should make a finding on the extent (if any) to which the order is punitive and explain how the order informed its exercise of the sentencing discretion.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.8 – Alcohol exclusion condition

refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.8 – Alcohol exclusion condition

title: CCO bond condition
statement: A bond secures compliance and may be forfeited on non-compliance; the court must consider whether the offender’s financial circumstances (per the pre-sentence report) support it and fix a time to pay. Repayment rules apply on cancellation, variation or expiry: within seven days (unless a longer period is ordered) if the CCO or bond is cancelled, varied or otherwise dealt with; otherwise, where the money is not liable to be forfeited, on the later of the listed events (one of which is three months after the CCO expires) — post-sentence administration, not a sentencing limit.

refs.q: The court may attach a condition requiring the offender to pay an amount of money as bond to ensure they comply with the CCO.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.9 – Bond condition

refs.q: When attaching a bond condition, the court must have regard to whether the offender’s financial circumstances (as contained in the pre-sentence report) are sufficient to support the payment of the bond and fix a period for the offender to pay.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.9 – Bond condition

refs.q: If the CCO or bond is cancelled, varied or otherwise dealt with, the Crown must repay the bond money to the offender within seven days, unless the court orders a longer period.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.9 – Bond condition

refs.q: • within three months of the expiry of the relevant CCO; or
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.9 – Bond condition

refs.q: In other circumstances where the money is not liable to be forfeited, the Crown must repay the offender, on the later of the following:

refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.9 – Bond condition

title: CCO judicial monitoring condition
statement: If the court is satisfied it is necessary to review compliance, it may direct court monitoring with review hearings (information, reports or tests may be required; no medical testing without consent); it may then cancel, vary or keep the condition; failure to re-appear may lead to an arrest warrant.

refs.q: If the court is satisfied that it is necessary for the court to review the offender’s compliance with a CCO during its course, it may attach a condition directing that the offender be monitored by the court.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.10 – Judicial monitoring condition

refs.q: However, a judicial monitoring condition does not empower the offender to be medically tested without their consent.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.10 – Judicial monitoring condition

refs.q: If an offender fails to re-appear for review in accordance with a judicial monitoring condition, the court may issue a warrant to arrest.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.10 – Judicial monitoring condition

refs.q: At the hearing a court may: • require or invite the offender to answer questions or provide information, including reports or the results of medical examinations or medical tests; • invite the offender’s medical practitioner to produce medical reports or the results of medical tests that concern the offender; and • require or invite information from the Secretary to the Department of Justice, the person who prosecuted the offender for the offence and any other person the court considers appropriate.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.10 – Judicial monitoring condition

refs.q: After conducting a review hearing, the court may cancel or vary the monitoring condition, including changing the duration of the condition, the timing of review hearings and the information that must be provided on future reviews. refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.10 – Judicial monitoring condition

refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.10 – Judicial monitoring condition

refs.q: A review hearing may be conducted by the judicial officer who imposed the CCO or another judicial officer of the same court.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.10 – Judicial monitoring condition

refs.q: It may also be conducted via videolink with the offender at a remote location if that promotes their best interests and rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.4 – Conditions > 11.4.2 – Discretionary conditions > 11.4.2.10 – Judicial monitoring condition

title: CCO justice plan condition (offenders with an intellectual disability)
statement: For an intellectually disabled offender the court may attach a justice plan condition directing participation in a plan of services. Before imposing it the court must consider a pre-sentence report, a statement from the DHS Secretary that the person has an intellectual disability, and a plan of available services; the Manual says both that the court “must request” the plan and that it “may request, and must consider” these materials (flag.justice_plan_request). The condition lasts for a specified period of less than two years or the period of the sentence, whichever is shorter. The court may direct a review at a specified time; if it does not, the Secretary must review the plan within a year and then at intervals of no more than a year. On application the court may confirm, vary or cancel the condition if the offender is no longer willing to comply, their needs are not being met, they have failed without reasonable excuse to comply, or the condition is no longer appropriate; on cancellation it may cancel the sentence and re-sentence, considering prior compliance.

title: CCO variation
statement: On application, the court may act if circumstances have materially altered so the offender cannot comply; circumstances were wrongly stated; consent is withdrawn; rehabilitation would be advanced; or continuation is unnecessary. It may confirm, cancel and re-sentence as if just found guilty, cancel with no further order, vary, alter conditions or programs. It must first assess the extent of compliance.

title: Sentencing on contravention of a CCO
statement: Contravention is a State offence; the court has the variation powers. Bond forfeiture may be ordered on variation or confirmation and must be ordered on cancellation. Account must be taken of compliance; non-compliance diminishes rehabilitation prospects and is relevant to specific deterrence. On cancellation the better course is to set aside the whole sentence and sentence afresh, declaring pre-sentence detention including time served; a custodial term longer than the original combination sentence would be a “very unusual case”. The Manual describes the breach offence only as one that “may attract a three-month term of imprisonment” (11.7.3); the offence register has no CCO-contravention row, so for a contravention charge the app asks the user to confirm the maximum.

refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 11 – Community correction order > 11.6 – Contravention

title: CCO and the purposes: all purposes achievable; community protection
statement: A CCO may achieve all the s 5(1) purposes (Boulton). Community-protection primacy for serious offenders does not apply to non-custodial CCOs but may bear on combining a CCO with imprisonment; protection is served by treatment conditions, but conditions cannot run longer than necessary merely to protect the community.

title: Purposes of dismissals, discharges and adjournments (release orders)
statement: For Victorian offences a court may, where a charge is proved, dismiss without conviction, discharge on conviction, or release on adjournment with or without conviction on an undertaking with conditions. These orders may be made to: provide for rehabilitation by serving the sentence in the community; take account of the trivial, technical or minor nature of the offence; allow the offender to demonstrate remorse as agreed with the court; allow for cases where recording a conviction, or more than nominal punishment, is not appropriate; or allow for other extenuating or exceptional circumstances justifying mercy. (app policy) A reasoning that proposes one of these orders should identify which purpose it serves.

Its purpose is to determine whether a temporary treatment order or court secure treatment order should be made. A community assessment order is in force for seven days from when it is made; an inpatient order expires seven days after the person is received at a designated mental health service. title: Court secure treatment orders: a distinct sentencing option; single orders for multiple offences
statement: Imposed on conviction; a distinct option — custody in a mental health service requires a court secure treatment order, not imprisonment with a direction on how it is served. The court must notify the authorised psychiatrist. Of the predecessor hospital security order (whose analyses likely still largely apply): the person was not excused from responsibility — detained because of a serious offence, not because of the illness. title: DATO activation and cancellation
statement: Activation only in the circumstances listed (s 18ZL(1)(f) sanction; cancellation for reoffending; s 18ZP(1)). The court first calculates the remaining custodial part and may order less but never more. The maximum remaining custodial part (both courts) is two years less the time the treatment and supervision part has operated if the original custodial part was no more than two years, otherwise the original custodial part less that time; within that maximum, declared custody and secure-custody sanction periods are deducted. The court weighs compliance (efforts, not mere time), the punitive aspects of compliance and earlier sanctions, and all the circumstances. An activation of one year or more may attract a non-parole period. Cancellation under s 18ZN(1) follows reoffending punishable by “at least 12 months” imprisonment (compare “more than 12 months” in 15A.2.2: flag.dato_cancellation_threshold). Cancellation under s 18ZP is a two-step discretionary process focused on events during the order; unwillingness to comply is distinct from a dependency-affected capacity to comply; it would be erroneous to treat s 18ZP(1)(c) as a power to sanction serious non-compliance, but repeated non-compliance may show that the order is not likely to achieve its purposes and so engage the power to cancel under s 18ZP(1)(d); re-sentencing after cancellation cannot be imprisonment; reasons are required for a decision that adversely affects the offender.

refs.q: The Drug Court can only activate the custodial part of a DATO under s 18ZE when it: • applies a sanction for non-compliance with a DATO condition under s 18ZL(1)(f), activating the custodial part for a period of between one and seven days • as a sanction for further offending cancels the treatment and supervision part under s 18ZN(1)(b)(i) or • cancels the treatment and supervision part under s 18ZP(1).

refs.q: When considering whether to activate a period shorter than the remaining custodial part the court must evaluate and consider a range of factors, including: • the nature of compliance and non-compliance by the offender. In doing so, compliance should not be equated with time subject to the order. In determining the extent of compliance the court should assess the offender’s efforts to rehabilitate and participate in the program, and evidence of any lack of effort and commitment. • recognising that an offender’s compliance with the treatment and supervision part of a DATO, despite its rehabilitative purpose, involves restrictions on the offender’s freedom and the imposition of positive obligations, and that any penalties previously imposed for breaches of the DATO themselves have a punitive aspect. • any other considerations relevant to sentencing, such as ‘all the circumstances’, ‘mitigating factors in general’ and what has occurred between the imposition of the DATO and the cancellation of the supervision and treatment part of the order.

refs.q: Secondly, the RSA provides that a court may disqualify a person from driving, or may cancel or suspend their license, where they have been found guilty or convicted of an offence under the RSA, or any other offence ‘in connection with the driving of a motor vehicle’.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 16 – Licence disqualification > 16.2 – Discretionary licence disqualification

refs.q: It commences when the order is imposed, or on any later date the court specifies.

title: Licence suspensions: presumption of concurrency; RSA Part 6B suspension taken into account
statement: A later suspension under the same specified provisions is presumed concurrent unless the court orders otherwise or the RSA requires consecutive periods; a Part 6B RSA suspension must be taken into account in fixing the period. (A presumption the court may displace and a matter to take into account: the auditor checks the reasoning addresses any current or Part 6B suspension recorded in intake.driving.)

refs.q: Where an offender’s driver licence or learner permit is already suspended under specified provisions and their driver licence or learner permit is later suspended under the same provisions, the later suspension is presumed to be concurrent with the earlier suspension unless the court orders otherwise.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 16 – Licence disqualification > 16.4 – Presumption of concurrency and interaction with the RSA

refs.q: This presumption does not apply if the RSA (or its regulations or rules) requires the suspension or disqualification to be consecutive.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 16 – Licence disqualification > 16.4 – Presumption of concurrency and interaction with the RSA

refs.q: Separately, if the person has had their driver licence or learner permit suspended under Part 6B of the RSA, and the court orders that: • their driver licence or learner permit is cancelled, and disqualifies them from obtaining one for a specified time; or • the person’s driver licence or learner permit is suspended; the court must take into account that period of suspension in fixing the period of suspension or disqualification.
